how-to-improve-speaking-skills-in-childr:
Fluent speaking rests on two things that have nothing to do with technique: having something to say, and having a listener who waits. Almost everything else follows from those.

Having something to say

A child who is not doing much, seeing much, or being told much has thin material. Speaking practice with nothing behind it produces performance rather than communication.

So the first move is not speaking practice at all. It is trips, books, jobs, arguments, obsessions and being read to above their level. Children with rich material speak fluently about it without being taught to.

Having a listener who waits

Five silent seconds after a question. No finishing their sentences, no supplying the word, no correcting the grammar while they are mid-thought. Every one of those teaches a child that speaking is monitored, and monitored speech gets shorter.

The three things worth practising directly

Explaining. The hardest and most useful. Ask a child to explain something they know well to somebody who does not know it. Explaining requires modelling what is missing from the other person's head, which is a genuine cognitive demand and the thing most adults are bad at.

Telling a story in order. Beginning, then what happened, then how it ended. Children commonly start in the middle and reverse. Prompting gently for order builds the structure that later shows up in their writing.

Real transactions. Ordering, asking, paying, phoning. Small, real, mildly uncomfortable, and worth more than any exercise because the stakes are genuine and the feedback is immediate.

What to do about filler and rambling

Mostly nothing, at least until around eleven. Filler words and a wandering structure are normal features of developing speech, and drawing attention to them makes a child self-conscious, which produces more of both.

If an older child wants to improve, record them once with their agreement and let them hear it. Self-noticing works where correction does not.

Volume and pace

Two mechanical things that make a large difference and are easy to practise as a game. Speak so the person furthest away can hear. Slow down, because everybody speeds up under pressure and a child under pressure speeds up more.

What quiet children need

Not encouragement to speak more, which raises the stakes. Smaller audiences, more warning, a defined role, and time. A shy child who is given a job at a gathering speaks considerably more than one who is urged to join in.

The check that matters

Not confidence or fluency, which vary by temperament and always will. Whether the child can make themselves understood to somebody who does not already know what they mean, and whether they notice when they have not.

That is a skill. Being outgoing is a personality trait, and confusing the two makes quiet children feel they have failed at something they have not.
storytelling-activities-for-kids:
Making stories builds sequence, memory, vocabulary and perspective at once, and children will do it for hours without being asked. Here are activities that get a child telling rather than reciting.

The round-robin story

One sentence each, round the table or the car. The rule that makes it work: you must connect to what came before. Chaos is fine. This is the easiest way in and it works from about four.

Three random objects

Pull three things out of a drawer. A spoon, a key, a sock. All three must appear in the story. Constraints make invention easier rather than harder, which surprises most children.

What happened next

Stop a familiar story before the end and ask them to finish it differently. Or start after the end: what did the wolf do the following week.

Tell it from the other side

The same events from the point of view of somebody else in the story, including the villain. This is perspective-taking with a plot attached, and it is genuinely demanding from about seven.

The family story

Tell a story about something that actually happened, before your child was born, involving people they know. These are the ones children ask for repeatedly, and they do something the invented ones do not: they place the child inside a line of people.

Story from a photograph

Any photograph with people in it. Who are they, what happened five minutes before, what happens next. Works well with old family photographs and with pictures of strangers.

The unreliable narrator

For older children. Tell the story as somebody who is getting it slightly wrong, and let the listener work out what really happened. Sophisticated, funny, and it teaches something about how accounts work.

Retelling as a job

After a film or a book, ask them to tell it to somebody who was not there. Retelling requires selecting what matters, which is a different skill from remembering.

Story dice, or cards

Draw three, use all three. The commercial versions are fine and a set of picture cards from anywhere works identically.

Two rules for all of them

No corrections. Not the plot holes, not the grammar, not the fact that the dragon was blue three minutes ago. Correction turns a story into a test.

You go first sometimes. A child who has heard an adult tell a bad, funny, made-up story on the spot understands that this is allowed to be rough. Modelling imperfection is most of what unlocks a self-conscious child.

Why it is worth the time

Oral storytelling predicts later writing more directly than early writing practice does. A child who can hold a story in their head and deliver it in order has the structure; putting it on paper is then a transcription problem rather than a composition one.

That is the underrated part. A great deal of what looks like a writing difficulty at eight is a child who has not yet had enough practice at building a story out loud.
how-storytelling-helps-child-development:
Story is not decoration on top of childhood. It is one of the main ways children work out how the world holds together, and it does several separable things at once.

Sequence and cause

A story is a chain: this happened, so that happened. Following one requires holding earlier events while processing later ones, and noticing that the connection is causal rather than merely successive.

That is not a small ask. It is the same structure that underlies explaining, planning and reasoning about consequences, and story is where children practise it first and most.

Other minds

Narrative is unusual in giving direct access to what somebody else thinks and wants, including when it differs from what is true. A child following a story in which one character does not know what the reader knows is doing sophisticated perspective work.

The association between narrative fiction and social understanding is one of the more consistent findings in this area, though as ever it is correlational and the direction is not perfectly clean.

Language beyond conversation

Books and told stories carry sentence structures and vocabulary that everyday speech does not. Even simple children's books use rarer words than ordinary adult conversation. This is why being read to matters for years after a child can read alone.

Memory, with a structure to hang on

Information in narrative form is remembered far better than the same information in a list. This is old and well established, and it is why oral traditions carried enormous amounts of material accurately for centuries.

It also means a child who learns something as a story keeps it.

Rehearsing difficulty at a safe distance

Children use stories to approach things they are not ready to meet directly: being lost, being left, being frightened, dying. The distance is what makes it bearable, and the repetition of a story a child asks for over and over is usually them working on something.

This is worth remembering when a child wants the same slightly frightening book for the eleventh time. They are not stuck; they are processing.

Belonging

Family stories do something the invented ones cannot. Research on family narratives suggests children who know stories about their family, including difficult ones, tend to show stronger resilience and sense of self. The plausible mechanism is that a child who knows their family has come through things has evidence that things can be come through.

Tell them the ones where it went wrong as well as the triumphs.

Being told is not the same as being read to

Worth distinguishing, because they do different work. Reading aloud carries the language of books. Telling, with no book, carries eye contact, improvisation and the sense that this person is making something for you right now. Children respond to told stories differently, and a parent who claims not to be able to tell stories is usually a parent who has not tried twice.

Both are worth doing. Neither requires any skill beyond willingness to be slightly bad at it in front of somebody who does not mind.
how-to-teach-public-speaking-to-kids:
Public speaking is mostly two things: managed nerves and rehearsed structure. Almost none of it is natural confidence, which is why children who look like naturals are usually children who have done it before.

What is reasonable to expect

Six to eight: a few sentences to a familiar group. Reading aloud something they wrote. Expect them to look at the paper the whole time, and let them.

Eight to eleven: a couple of minutes on something they know about, with notes. This is the age where a talk about their own obsession works far better than an assigned topic.

Eleven to fourteen: five minutes, structured, with an argument in it. Also the age when self-consciousness peaks, so expect a step backwards even from a child who was fine at nine.

Fourteen and up: proper preparation, handling questions, adjusting when it is not landing.

The structure that always works

Three parts, and it is worth teaching once and reusing.

Say what you are going to talk about and why anybody should care. Then three points, no more, each with one example. Then say what you said and stop.

Children over-plan the middle and neglect the ending, so the talk trails off. Rehearse the last sentence until it is automatic; a clean ending makes the whole thing feel competent.

Rehearsal is the actual technique

Not reading it through in their head. Out loud, standing, at full volume, several times, until they are not searching for the next sentence.

Most of the fear is of drying up. Rehearsal removes the thing being feared, which is more effective than any amount of reassurance about it.

Then build the audience: the wall, one parent, two people, a grandparent on a call, the class.

The physical part

Teach it as mechanics rather than confidence, because mechanics can be practised.

Breathe out longer than in before starting. Feet flat, weight even. Hold the notes, or something, because hands are the thing children do not know what to do with. Speak slower than feels right. Look at three friendly faces in different parts of the room rather than trying to look at everybody.

What not to say beforehand

"Don't be nervous." Nerves are appropriate and unavoidable, and telling a child not to have them adds failure to fear.

Better: everybody feels this, including people who are good at it, and it fades about thirty seconds in. That is true, and it gives them something to wait for.

Afterwards

Ask what they noticed before offering anything. Then name one specific thing that went well and, only if they want it, one thing to try next time.

A child who is given five improvements has learned that it went badly, whatever you said about the first one.

The aim at this age is not a polished speaker. It is a child who has discovered that the feeling is survivable and that preparation is what makes it so.
